utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth. Good morning to the interpreters, members of the registry, the Prosecution. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-97-24-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May we have the appearances? For the Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Susan Somers, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I have the honour of presenting the group which has facilitated the amendment, and I wish to do so. Miss Helen Long, Mr. Andrew Corin, our new member of the team, Mr. Massimo Scaliotti, Suellen Taylor, of course Denise Gustin. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Good morning, Dr. Stakic. We are here today, in this hearing today to hear the Prosecution's application for leave to amend the indictment, so we will proceed as follows: We will hear the arguments, and then we'll see what the Defence's answer is, and then you may have a reply by the Prosecutor then, if the Prosecution has a response. Mrs. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The application sets forth, among other points, the fact that from the inception, as early as 1997 in front of Her Honour Odio-Benito, there has been an indication of intent to amend the indictment if - once and if the accused were taken into custody. Only in 2001 was the accused Stakic taken into custody. His status as an accused, having been on a sealed indictment, was not changed in terms of the counts when the case against Milan Kovacevic, co-accused, was amended. However, many, if not all, of the points which would have been in the accusation against, or were in the accusation against Kovacevic have been incorporated one way or the other into the present indictment, amended indictment, for which we are seeking to -- upon which we're seeking to proceed. The initial indictment set forth a complicity in genocide count alone; however, the factual base for that complicit in genocide count was broad. It included, in terms of crime base, principally Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje camps. It set forth essentially the same factual background which has been elaborated upon in the, the current amended indictment which we are seeking to proceed upon. We have had the benefit, since the 1997 indictment, of new materials seized from the various organs of the Republika Srpska in Prijedor and Banja Luka which have given us much greater insight into the alleged criminal activity of the accused and which figure into this indictment. The time frame incorporates the period in the original indictment, however, we have been able to ascertain sufficient evidence to take it back to September 1st -- I'm sorry, September 11, 1991, and extend it to September 30, 1992. This case does differ from, for example, the Omarska and Keraterm cases in that that is a political leadership case at the municipal level. However, the activity that was conducted by the political leadership in Prijedor municipality was reflected in the crime base in Omarska. So the allegations that are set forth in the original indictment again reflect, perhaps on a lower scale because it was done under a different set of circumstances, the essential political scene, at least set out to put the Defence on notice as to what type of facts we'll be relying on, it is expanded upon in the proposed amended indictment. The counts that have been added include the complicity in genocide count, along with a genocide count itself; murder, crime against humanity; extermination, crime against humanity; murder, violation of the laws and customs of war; persecutions, crime against humanity; torture, crime against humanity; cruel treatment, violation of the laws and customs of war; torture, violation of the laws and customs of war; deportation, crime against humanity; wanton destruction of cities, towns, and villages, violation of the laws and customs of war; and lastly, destruction or wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion, violation of the laws and customs of war. These counts were built upon a great number of the facts in the original indictment, plus through the work of my team. The information or the evidence, as we consider it to be, gathered from other sources, including the searches, and evidence that has surfaced through the other trials that have arisen out of the operative facts on Prijedor, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and certainly the very well-developed base that came out of Tadic. The actual time frame, should the Bench grant our application, for trial would, I believe, not be greatly expanded from what would have been necessary in the original count because the original count was the overall -- all facts in a complicity in genocide count, and we think we can try to keep the case tightly tried, with the assistance, of course, of the use of judiciously noticed facts and stipulations that we have discussed at prior Status Conferences. Although this is a Rule 50 amendment with -- before the Chamber, it appears that confirmation is not the issue from the Rules but, rather, whether or not it is a new indictment, and, in fact, we believe that it is soundly an amendment as contemplated by the Rule. We have -- should the Chamber wish, we have the materials which have served, as it were, supporting materials for any additional aspects of the charges which may not have been included in the original supporting materials for the single complicity in genocide count. We would leave them with the Registry for the Chamber. It is a single set, unredacted, and we'd be very happy if the Chamber would wish to see these materials. If not, we of course leave that in the Chamber's hands. If I may answer any further questions. I believe we have set forth requirements of the Rule and believe that there is no aspect of this which would cause surprise to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Ms. Somers. The Judges might have questions towards the end of the proceedings, but we want to give the parties the opportunity of -- to give some more explanations. Mr. Lukic, can you answer the Prosecutor's arguments? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you know, Your Honours, we haven't seen the indictment yet, the amended indictment, so -- although we have the indictment for late Dr. Kovacevic. So I think that in general we know what this amended indictment is about, but still, we would like to see it to be able to answer any further questions. And our position is that this is a new indictment, not amended indictment, because adding 11 counts on one makes really something new, not something broadened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, how much time would you need to look at the new or amended indictment, in your version, that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that we need more than half an hour because, as I said, we have the indictment for late Dr. Kovacevic, and we suppose that it's basically the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Registrar, has the indictment been sent to Mr. Lukic, and why has not the indictment been sent to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, if no one has received a copy of the Prosecution's application and the amended indictment. It was, however, distributed yesterday, for the information I have, to all the parties, including the Chamber. But I'll try to follow this problem and see what happened and why it seems that it hasn't been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the question is whether Mr. Lukic already has an indictment, an amended indictment, that is, again. I can see that you have the answer to this, Mrs. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may assist the Chamber, Your Honour, the actual application, along with the indictment, was filed confidentially, partially ex parte. The Rule requires that there be a hearing by the parties on the application but does not indicate that the actual indictment be provided until the Chamber has made a ruling on the application as to whether or not it would be appropriate. I have, however, sent to Mr. Lukic in advance a -- the draft of the application for amendment so that he has been on notice about what the additional counts would be. We have spoken telephonically about the event -- I'm sorry, about the amended indictment and the counts, so there was notice as soon as we were able to reach Mr. Lukic after he returned from his vacation. The documents were in fact distributed yesterday, and if they have not reached Chambers, I'm concerned, but we did physically bring them down for distribution, and for this I can offer no explanation. If the Chamber normally would break -- although, in fact, I must say that the experience has been that it is not customary to give out the amended indictment until the Chamber has heard us on it, and then if the application is granted, it is provided, with my understanding, normally a break to allow the accused and his counsel to confer for purposes of entering a subsequent plea. However, we are in the Chamber's hands in terms of the procedure here. The indictment was not provided, only a copy of the application which details the charges but not, of course, any of the summary of the evidence on it -- of the facts underlying it, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, at what point, then, in this process would somebody like Mr. Lukic, the Defence counsel, have an opportunity to make his argument that it is -- to make his argument that it is not, in fact, merely an amendment but a new -- I mean, does -- what is your interpretation of the Rules that would allow -- when is the window of opportunity for him to make that argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the Rule does not really address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it has been -- at this point, just beginning to be interpreted. But in the past, the application details at least enough counts to indicate how much, if any, other activity would be added to the existing indictment. Now, again, the detail is not there, but it has not in the past been there. And I don't know whether this Chamber wishes to initiate its own procedure and permit some type of initial reading just to know enough detail to enter a plea, although, again, there seems to be enough precedent that this has not been the case. Some Chambers do; some Chambers don't. And however the Chamber wishes us to do it, we followed the approach that has been consistent with past practice. But again, Rule 50's changes with the lack of confirmation once it is before the Chamber perhaps requires some consideration other than -- but our position has been that there is no entitlement to see it in advance, that it is sufficient to know the additional charges and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But what's the, what's the difference? Now, suppose, just suppose his argument were accepted, "But gee, when you add 11 new counts to one count, you're really doing more than amending the indictment; you're creating a new one." The consequence of that would be what? That he'd have to get it -- that the indictment would have to be reconfirmed or confirmed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- with supporting material? If that argument were accepted. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it were a new, if it were truly a new indictment incorporating other municipalities, a time frame that went into 1995. But it is not. This is the indictment from the period. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question to you which I was going to ask but it's part of this now, is, can you tell us whether or not the new counts are based on new incidents, new episodes that the old count was not based on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are some additional killings resulting from attacks that -- well, because Keraterm and Omarska and Trnopolje were the results of these attacks, I would feel relatively safe in saying that the attacks would have been presented one way or the other, it's a question -- because most of the detentions and any resulting deaths or violations of Article 5 would arise either from these attacks or from activity in the camps. So there would not be a substantial increase. There may be some locations that would not have appeared necessarily in the camp cases because some of it -- because of some of the killings which occurred outside of the camps. We do deal with killings outside of camps here as well. This, I think, is significant for the Chamber to know. And, Your Honour, also, of course, there is the fact that this individual occupied a position of control and authority in perhaps a different way, a political level that was not present. However, it is its impact on the crime base that is crucial, and the crime base is very much based on the same facts, with some expansions, as the camp cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Somers, I personally want to go to the merits of the application you've filed, but you have a preliminary procedural issue to deal with. What we find in Rule 50, paragraph (C), is that the Prosecutor may amend the indictment once the case has been assigned to a Trial Chamber with leave of that Trial Chamber or a Judge of that Chamber after having heard the parties. In other words, the application gives rise to a discussion between the two parties, the Prosecution and the Defence. Hence my question: How could the Defence be heard, take part in this discussion if it doesn't know what the indictment is? What we had beforehand, as you know, is that the application for leave to amend was presented to the Confirmation Judge and, thereafter, once the Confirming Judge had confirmed the indictment, it was sent to the Defence, the accused would appear in the courtroom, and he or she would already know the contents of the amended indictment. Now, following the latest change to the Rules, I believe, but I'd like to seek your views on this, I think that we find ourselves in a new proceeding; that is that the Chamber is to rule after having heard the parties. I interpret this as meaning that there is a discussion between two parties. Therefore, for the Defence to be able to take part in this discussion, it must be informed. So what do you think regarding this reading of the Rules, and more specifically, as to the issue of what it means to have heard the parties first? What do you think, Mrs. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on, for example, the amendment of the Kordic indictment in 1998, the only aspect of hearing the parties was, again, on the application, there was no presentation in advance of the indictment. I'm trying to recollect without having my notes in front of me, but I was part of that. And the actual indictment was presented only to a Confirming Judge after the Trial Chamber heard the application on amendment. So it was not a noticed or an adversarial matter up front to have the indictment distributed. I do not see that it was contemplated that there would be a debate about the substance. I believe that would be more for the Chamber to consider, as it was considered in the older proceedings, that the Chamber might take a look, and it may give its decision on whether or not it believed it was beyond or an absolutely new instrument, charging instrument. And if the Chamber so believed, then it would order accordingly and it would go into a confirmation proceeding. But that -- there is no real provision for an assessment as to whether or not the Defence agrees with whether these things should be in. That was really a decision for the Trial Chamber. And then if it so decided, then the instrument was presented to the Defence and the plea would be entered. At that time, it did revert to the Confirming Judge. I don't recall a provision for it coming before the Chamber at that point in time. It was sent back to the Confirming Judge. But there seems to have been, if I read it correctly, a change in procedure, and again, it becomes a matter for the Chamber to determine if it sees it as truly an amendment, and if so, to act on the application, and then it is given to the Defence for the same procedure. It almost looks as if this were an administrative facilitation tool, but it does not seem to alter the, as it were, ex parte nature of the decision as to whether or not it is a new indictment. I see no evidence of that in the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Somers, you did not answer my question. How do you understand the notion of hearing the parties of the adversarial system which is couched in the Rule? You've mentioned the Kordic case law, but what happened in the Kordic case, that was before the Rules were changed. Now we have this new Rule which clearly specifies that the Chamber is to hear the parties first. So what do you mean by that, by this adversarial procedure? How do you read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it as going to the leave to amend and what is set forth in the motion, not necessarily the accompanying document. I do not see that it really changes the initial assessment by the Chamber as to whether or not it believes it to be a new one. There may be factors which the Defence wishes to bring to our attention about the counts, but it does not, by its plain language, suggest that the indictment is distributed before there is a decision to -- as to whether or not it is the appropriate subject of an amendment and allowing the indictment as an amendment to be the document in force. I believe that it goes to just the hearing on the application for leave, not on the substance of the actual charges. That was the purpose for laying out the expanded charges and indicating if there were a change in the time period, which was done in the application. I think that is sufficient for the Defence to answer this part of the proceeding. I do not think it goes beyond that. I see no evidence of intent taken beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But surely, Ms. Somers, suppose we were later on in the proceeding than we are now and the Prosecution came in and said, as can happen, "We want to add six or seven new counts to that," and we had already begun trial or something? Surely the Rules would envision having a hearing in which a Trial Chamber could say, "Sorry. We're well along into this. It's not fair to everybody involved. It's too late. You can't amend it this dramatically."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I mean, there has got to be room for the Trial Chamber, once the procedure has got under way, to look at at least what is being asked of in the application proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would seem from prior practice that if the case were already commenced, with witnesses having been sworn and evidence taken, that could change the equation. We are not at that phase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I think because we are at the phase at which we find ourselves, the -- what I would call the more traditional approach that I think seems to stand intact in this Rule would apply, that the Chamber would take a look at the indictment and make a decision and then grant, hopefully, the application, hopefully, and then proceed. But I -- at the stage at which we find ourselves, I don't think there would be any reason to, even in the interests of justice, have an assessment of anything in the substance of it by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Before ruling on this issue, on this procedural issue, I'd like to give Mr. Lukic the opportunity to speak because we've come up with new factors and you might have something to say on this. You have the floor, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't think that I have to add much because basically Your Honours have already put all questions I had, and I think that it's up to the Chamber to decide on this matter. And according to my learned friend, I shouldn't interfere too much in this matter, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has to rule on the issue of whether the notion of having heard the parties as stated in Rule 50 of the Rules means that the Defence must be heard on the application filed by the Prosecutor for leave to amend the indictment. The Trial Chamber rules that the words "having heard the parties" means that the Trial Chamber has to hear the parties before it rules; "the parties," meaning the Prosecutor and the Defence. Therefore, the Trial Chamber rules that the Prosecutor's application for leave to amend must be notified to the Defence. The Defence will have 45 minutes. Mr. Lukic asked for 30 minutes, but we grant him 45 minutes in which he can look at the application, upon which we shall return to the courtroom to hear the Defence on the application. We are going to suspend the hearing for 45 minutes. Did you want to have less time, Mrs. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just want a clarification. The application itself was served upon the Defence. It was simply not the indictment. As long as -- I want to make sure the Chamber knows, we still hold the indictment and will wait to turn it over until there has been a hearing on the application. Is that -- do I understand Your Honour correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. For us, the application is the application and its annex because the application without the indictment doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the entire application with the annex.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Therefore, it is up to the Registry to make sure that the Defence will have the entire application. Do you agree, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we're going to have a break of 45 minutes. --- Break taken at 10.42 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. In keeping with the decision made by the Trial Chamber, we are going to hear the Defence, according to the Rules, and the interpretation of the Trial Chamber by the Rules. We believe that the English version is clearer than the French version. There are some differences, because the English version says clearly that this, after having heard the parties. And if you look at Rule 2, which defines the parties, the parties are the Prosecutor and the Defence. [In English] If you put this definition of Article 2 into Article 50, we'll have the same result saying, "... after having heard the Prosecutor and the Defence." [Interpretation] There we are. We're now going to hear the Defence. Mr. Lukic, how do you view the Prosecutor's application?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that we hold the same position, that actually in front of us we have a completely new indictment, which is based on different factual ground than the previous one, although we, as I said, expected this indictment, which is almost the same as the indictment of late Dr. Kovacevic. But as I said, we think our position is that it's a completely new indictment, and I think that we should proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what difference would it make in terms of the Defence's preparation or getting ready to defend whether or not we decided that it was a new indictment or an amended indictment? I mean, we're at a very early stage now. So what real difference would it make to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are right. We are still preparing anyway, so we are in process of preparation. And of course, having 11 new counts in the indictment, it's clear that we will need more time for preparation, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I think Rule 50(C) takes care of that to further extent. It says you have "... a further period of thirty days [for] preliminary motions ... and, where necessary, the date for trial may be postponed to ensure adequate time for the preparation of the defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the trial date hasn't been established yet so it doesn't affect us much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mrs. Somers, do you have anything to say in reply? So basically, the Defence says that we are dealing with a totally new factual base, so this is a radically new indictment, this is not an amended indictment. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I submit that the response of the Defence is groundless. In fact, just looking back at what transpired with the Kovacevic situation, it was granted. The amendment was granted. Further, because in this instance genocide or complicity in genocide was the initial very large charge, almost -- well, arguably every fact that is now -- instead of just made a bit of evidence that would go into inferring the genocidal intent, has been broken out or crystallised into separate -- into different counts which is the -- within the prerogative of the Prosecutor. We think, given the levels of intent that have to be shown, this is the wise course to do and was, in fact, followed in Kovacevic. But the factual submissions which we would have to make at trial would be these factual submissions to enable the Chamber to make a decision which it will still have to make on the genocide counts, and there is really no substantial variation. The additional month at the end is to cover a period of time where we can show, based on, again, the ability to know better about this individual than was known earlier, activity going through the end of September. And he is alleged, in the accused's section of the 1997 indictment, to be a member of the Crisis Staff. Again, we have to show that. We have set the time period that we are looking at to prove his positions of responsibility as 11 September, based on documentary evidence. But these facts as submitted would have had to have gone into the original count, the original genocide. It is, given the growing body, we hope, of law on genocide, perfectly normal and prudent to want to break out separate counts should there, for example, not be a conviction on complicity on genocide. But these facts at all times were the same or essentially the same facts that would have gone into proving the larger, more grave charge. We see no, no basis for a comment that it is a new indictment in the sense of new types of facts. It's a matter of proof. Again, reminding the Chamber, which I know it knows well, that Rule 72 provides a full opportunity for comments on or objections to form of indictment, which is traditionally where objections would appear, not at this time. This again -- these are legal issues about timing, but they are not issues where facts should be delved into now by the Defence. If there's further on the matter I may answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that should we, should we, the Chamber, at some point think it was a new indictment, you had confirmation material available for us; but if we decide it's an amended indictment, then the Defence -- which the Defence, if it were a new indictment, would get that confirmation material under 66, but it won't get it under an amendment, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, because the Rule is drafted in such a way that it says no longer is a confirmation required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- strictly speaking, legally they're not entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We -- should we choose to call witnesses, particular witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- yes, we would -- they would get them. And we are encouraging -- we hope we may engage in Rule 66 types of requests which we hope will speed things up. But again, I want to make it clear that whether we had to prove the count of genocide or all of the things that go into genocide, it is our burden. The time frame is basically the same. I disagree with Mr. Lukic that it's a longer trial. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I have a question that I'd like to put to Mr. Lukic. You may know that we are now with an indictment which was initially involving three co-accused. Two of these co-accused have now died. We therefore have this indictment against Mr. Stakic. As you can see, in the Kovacevic indictment, the Prosecutor added, I believe, 13 counts, and as you know, this gave rise to a decision, a ruling by the Trial Chamber, which has always regarded this indictment as an amended indictment. Never was the issue raised of knowing whether it was a new indictment. In this instant case, the Prosecutor is adding 11 counts. So basically, at the end of the day, the difference is that in this case, the Prosecutor did not include offences under Article 2, sort of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. If you compare the Kovacevic indictment with the Stakic indictment, and if you look at the way the Trial Chamber dealt with this issue in the Kovacevic case, do you still believe that you're dealing with a new indictment rather than with an amended one? What is your feeling to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, although knowing the decision, previous decision of the Trial Chamber in Kovacevic case, I can't escape the feeling that this is really a new indictment. I know that it's -- I leave it to the discretion of the Trial Chamber, but I have to think in a way according to the legal system from which I come from, and in our system, if you add so many counts to one count you had before, it's a new indictment; it's not amended. But if this Trial Chamber still holds the same position as the Trial Chamber in Kovacevic case, I would like to have Prosecution ordered to disclose the materials which follow this, according to them, amended indictment. So at least in that field to have covered the defence and to have provided the Defence with all materials necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two remarks on this. I can see the transcript which mentions the Kovacevic Trial Chamber, but in fact, I think we should refer to the Appeals Chamber. Is that what you mean, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second remark: I do understand your argument. You allude to your national legal system. Me too. I have a similar legal system, but we have to operate on the basis of the Tribunal's Rules. We do not work on a national basis. We cannot apply national rules to this Tribunal. But we understand your position, and we'll take it into account. Thank you. You may sit down, Mr. Lukic. Mrs. Somers, I have another question for you. You rely in your application on at least two arguments. You have the fact that the Prosecution's investigations have been maintained and have continued, that you have received additional materials from other cases. This is my question: If you compare the Kovacevic indictment to the present indictment for Stakic - I think we'll end up agreeing and saying that we're dealing with one single initial indictment - what is the difference between the Kovacevic indictment and that filed against Stakic if we leave aside the issue of violations or breaches to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly, we -- we're able to be more precise now as to the nature of the criminal responsibility or the alleged criminal responsibility of the accused Stakic with the benefit of having more materials. I'm confident that had he been included on the amendment for Kovacevic, we would have proceeded, but again, we are in a better position because of the other factors which we've indicated in our application. The nature of the -- the Kovacevic indictment was also adding genocide, crimes against humanity, violations of laws or customs of war and removing grave breaches. There is not a substantial difference in terms of the scope of the -- the breakdown of the counts. Again, these points would have been facts to have been proven. We have been able to crystallise them, regroup them into counts, which I think is a better practice, particularly in this institution given the state of -- trying to develop the jurisprudence on genocide. But the difference in charges, there was -- the allegations in Kovacevic discussed attacks. They were not terribly specific. They discussed deportation. They discussed the types of atrocities that took place in the camps. Again, this is what is merely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you, Mrs. Somers. So in conclusion, if you look at the two indictments, there's no substantial difference. Is that the conclusion we can draw? Is that what I heard from you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Essentially it tracks -- essentially, and I would want to make that clear, because certainly we have the benefit of detail and we have an expanded beginning by a couple of months and expanded end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question, Mrs. Somers. Why did you not include the breaches to the Geneva Conventions as that being a major difference between the two indictments?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a prosecutorial decision. The nature of proof that would have had to have been adduced, it would not have added greatly to dealing with this particular individual. It would not have made the difference that it has made in other cases. Specifically to this case, it would not have enhanced it greatly. And we've covered the facts, Your Honour, in the other counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer raises another question. Is the Prosecution going to take out infractions or offences under Rule 2 or Article 2 in other cases this Tribunal is going to hear, just for the sake of consistency?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It depends, Your Honour. That again depends on the type of proof that is available in every case, and it will vary. There are times when it is absolutely appropriate, if the proof is there, to proceed if the Prosecution wishes go on a grave breach that may not be touched upon by another type of count. That is very much individualistic, and I don't think that it would necessarily require a declaration of consistency because it would be so case specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But if it's a matter of proof, what is the difference between the Brdjanin and Talic case and this case when this comes to proof?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe there were factors above and beyond the Prosecution, if I'm correct, in the Brdjanin and Talic case, wherein Article 2 was added. I don't believe initially it was in the indictment, if I'm not wrong. I have to reserve that, but I think it was added. Again, I could be wrong, but I don't think -- that is a regional case. There may be points of proof with which I am not familiar in that case. I'm looking at a municipal leader, and for purposes of the municipal level, we felt strategically this was the soundest way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. We don't have any more questions. We're going to have a break, but before doing so, let me turn to Mr. Lukic. Are you ready to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty today? What is the position of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we are ready to enter the plea today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. We're going to have a break, a half-hour break. Were the Trial Chamber to grant the Prosecution's application, in that case we will move straight away to the initial appearance. So we're going to have a break for half an hour. --- Break taken at 11.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Somers, before I give the ruling, I would seek some clarification. I understood that you said you were available to disclose to the Defence, as it were, the supporting materials, the documents in support of a possible change to the indictment. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Within the time frame that we are allotted, yes, we are, Your Honour. Again, because it's not clear whether we have to, but we would do it, we'd ask the Chamber for the usual permission to make the redactions that are necessary to protect regular factors, but yes, we would be glad to do that within 30 days after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, yes, we could solve this issue without having to issue a ruling. What we had in mind, Ms. Somers, Mr. Lukic, is this: After the change made to Rule 50, which made it possible to look again at the indictment as amended by a Trial Chamber who has -- which has been assigned to the case and not by a Confirming Judge, I think that the Trial Chamber, looking at the overall Rules, has the same function as the Confirming Judge before. Therefore, once the amended indictment has been confirmed, you still have to disclose the supporting materials. We are therefore in the same position. We're basically doing the same work as the work done before by the Confirming Judge, so we should proceed in the same way as before. Mr. Lukic asked for something. You seem to agree. So the Chamber basically clarifies the issue and is now going to issue a ruling on this. But the Chamber uses this opportunity to clarify the situation to say that basically everything should be taking place as though it was a Confirming Judge who had confirmed a change to the indictment. We're now issuing our ruling. The Prosecutor filed an application for the leave to amend the indictment against Milomir Stakic. This change is reflected in the addition of 11 counts. The Defence opposed the application, stating that this is not tantamount to an amendment but that it is basically a totally new indictment. After hearing the parties on the issue, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecutor has a potential right to amend the indictment. The Prosecutor may therefore exercise the said right which may be also viewed as an obligation within the confines of the Rules, and more specifically, of Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber is also of the view that this is an amendment and this is not a new indictment. Indeed, the trial has not yet begun or come to an end, and the indictment must contain all the charges brought against the accused who needs more time to prepare for his defence before the trial begins. This being so and taking Rule 50 into account, the Trial Chamber grants the Prosecutor's application and thereby grants the requested amendment.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Motion Hearing adjourned at
